html:
An imperial mosque on the second hill of Istanbul, at the gate of the Grand Bazaar and just north of the Column of Constantine. Sultan Mahmud I began it in 1748 and his brother Osman III finished it in 1755, giving it its name, "the light of Osman". It was the first sultan's mosque in the city since the Blue Mosque, more than a century before, and the first great Ottoman building in the new Baroque style taken from Europe.

Its architect, Simeon Kalfa, was a Greek Christian, the first non-Muslim put in charge of a major imperial building; his chief assistant and most of the masons were Christians too. A single dome 25.4 m wide and 43.5 m high, the third largest historic dome in the city after Hagia Sophia and the Süleymaniye, rises on four great arches pierced with windows, a form close to Sinan's Mihrimah Sultan Mosque. Iron bracing runs up through the walls to the dome.

Look for the Baroque details: curving pediments, round and many-curved arches instead of pointed ones, a carved sunburst over the courtyard gate, and friezes of acanthus where earlier mosques had stalactite niches. The courtyard is horseshoe-shaped, a form never used in an Ottoman mosque before. The complex includes an oval library that opened with 5,031 books, a madrasa, a kitchen for the poor, and a private wing with a ramp up to the sultan's loge. A restoration from 2010 to 2012 found a large cistern beneath it.
